short: Buying and selling the same or an equivalent asset in different markets at once to profit from a price gap, with little or no risk.
kid: One friend sells sweets for one coin, and another friend will pay two coins for them. You buy from the first, sell to the second, and keep the extra coin.
detail: Arbitrage is the simultaneous purchase and sale of the same, or an economically equivalent, asset to capture a price difference. Pure arbitrage needs no net investment and carries no market risk, because both legs are locked in at the same moment; the person who does it is an arbitrageur. Classic forms include one share quoted at different prices on two exchanges, futures priced away from spot plus carrying cost, and currency cross-rates that do not line up. Arbitrage matters because it keeps related prices consistent: as arbitrageurs buy the cheap side and sell the dear one, the gap closes, which is the law of one price at work. In India, arbitrage mutual funds earn the gap between cash and futures prices. The common confusion is that real-world arbitrage is rarely risk-free: execution delays, costs, funding and counterparty problems can turn a sure thing into a loss.
example: Say ABC Ltd's shares are quoted at ₹500 on one exchange and ₹502 on another at the same instant. An arbitrageur who buys 1,000 shares on the first (₹5,00,000) and sells 1,000 on the second (₹5,02,000) locks in ₹2,000 before costs. If brokerage and taxes total ₹600, the net profit is ₹1,400.
formula: Arbitrage profit = Selling price in the dearer market − Buying price in the cheaper market − Transaction costs

short: Buying an asset today and selling a futures contract on it when the futures price is higher than today's price plus holding costs.
kid: You buy a toy today for five coins and promise a friend you will sell it to her next week for seven. Keeping it safe costs one coin, so you still end up one coin ahead.
detail: Cash-and-carry arbitrage exploits a futures price that is too high relative to its fair value. The trader buys the asset in the spot (cash) market, sells the futures contract and holds, or carries, the asset until expiry, when the futures price converges to the spot price. The profit is the futures premium minus the cost of carry: financing, storage and insurance, less any dividends or income received. The reverse cash-and-carry does the opposite when futures are too cheap: sell the asset short, buy futures and invest the sale proceeds. These trades anchor futures prices to the cost-of-carry model. In India, arbitrage mutual funds and proprietary desks run the trade on stock futures every month. A common confusion: the futures premium alone is not profit. If it merely equals the financing cost there is nothing to earn, and the short leg of a reverse trade can be costly or restricted.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at ₹1,000 in the cash market and its one-month future at ₹1,012. A trader buys 500 shares for ₹5,00,000 and sells one 500-share futures contract; at expiry the prices converge, locking in (1,012 − 1,000) × 500 = ₹6,000. If financing the purchase costs 0.6% for the month (₹3,000), the net gain is ₹3,000 before transaction costs.
formula: Fair futures price = Spot price × (1 + r × t) − Income received; Cash-and-carry profit per unit = Market futures price − Fair futures price

short: Buying or selling something to profit from guessing where its price goes next, accepting the risk of being wrong.
kid: You swap your sticker for a friend's because you think everyone will want hers tomorrow. If you guess right you can swap it for something better; if not, you lose out.
detail: Speculation is deliberately taking price risk to earn a profit from an expected move, as opposed to hedging, which reduces a risk you already have. A speculator may buy futures expecting a rise, sell them expecting a fall, or trade currencies, commodities or shares on a short-term view. Derivatives make speculation cheaper because only margin is posted, so gains and losses are leveraged. Speculators are useful: they take the other side of hedgers' trades, add liquidity and help prices absorb new information. Heavy leveraged speculation can amplify bubbles and crashes, which is why regulators set margins and position limits; SEBI tightened rules on index derivatives in late 2024 after its studies showed most individual F&O traders lose money. The common confusion: speculation is not the same as manipulation or pure gambling. It is legal risk-taking based on a view, though the line blurs when people trade without analysis.
example: Say a speculator buys one futures contract on ABC Ltd covering 500 shares at ₹800, posting margin of ₹80,000 (20% of the ₹4,00,000 contract value). If the price rises to ₹840, the gain is ₹20,000, a 25% return on the margin. If it falls to ₹760, the loss is also ₹20,000, a quarter of the money put up.

short: A situation where one side's gain exactly equals the other side's loss, so the total of gains and losses adds up to zero.
kid: When two friends share one cake, a bigger slice for one means a smaller slice for the other. The cake itself never gets any bigger.
detail: A zero-sum game is one in which the total of all participants' gains and losses is zero: every rupee one side wins, another side loses. Futures, forwards, options and swaps are zero-sum between the two parties to the contract, because the buyer's profit is precisely the seller's loss. Once brokerage, exchange fees, taxes and bid-ask spreads are counted, derivatives trading as a whole is negative-sum for traders. That helps explain why a SEBI study published in 2024 found that about 93% of individual F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24. The common confusion is to call the stock market zero-sum. Owning shares is positive-sum over the long run, because companies create value through earnings and dividends, so long-term shareholders can all gain together. A derivative creates no new value of its own; it reallocates risk between parties, which is still useful for hedgers.
example: Say Asha buys a futures contract on 100 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹1,000 from Ravi. If the price ends at ₹1,050, Asha gains ₹5,000 and Ravi loses ₹5,000, so the total is zero. If each also pays ₹200 in costs, the two of them are together ₹400 worse off.

short: An agreement to buy or sell an index, such as the Nifty 50, at a set level on a future date, settled in cash.
kid: Instead of guessing about one apple, you guess whether the whole basket of fruit will cost more or less next month. Whoever guesses wrong gives the other some coins.
detail: Index futures are exchange-traded futures whose underlying is a stock index rather than a single share. Because an index cannot be delivered, they are cash-settled: at expiry, gains and losses are paid on the difference between the contract price and the final index value, multiplied by the lot size, and daily mark-to-market moves money between buyers and sellers. Fund managers use them to hedge or quickly adjust market exposure, arbitrageurs keep them close to fair value, and traders use them for a leveraged view on the market. In India, BSE and NSE launched index futures in June 2000, and Nifty and Bank Nifty contracts are among the most traded; GIFT Nifty trades for most of the day and night. A common confusion: US headlines saying stock futures or Dow futures are up refer to index futures, which hint at where the market may open, not to single-stock contracts.
example: Say an index future trades at 20,000 with a lot size of 50 units (illustrative figures; exchanges revise lot sizes), so one contract is worth 20,000 × 50 = ₹10 lakh. If the future rises 200 points to 20,200, the buyer gains 200 × 50 = ₹10,000 and the seller loses the same amount.
formula: Profit on a long contract = (Exit level − Entry level) × Lot size

short: An agreement to buy or sell a set number of shares of one company at a fixed price on a future date.
kid: You and a friend agree today that next month you will buy ten of her marbles at a price you both pick now, whatever marbles cost by then.
detail: Stock futures, or single stock futures, are exchange-traded futures on one company's shares. Each contract covers a fixed lot of shares and expires on a set monthly date; traders post margin rather than the full value, and positions are marked to market daily. India has one of the world's most active single stock futures markets, launched in November 2001. Under the rules as of 2025, contracts held to expiry are physically settled (phased in during 2018-19), so the buyer must take delivery of the shares and the seller must deliver them. Only stocks that meet SEBI's size and liquidity criteria have futures. They are used for leveraged bets on a company, hedging a shareholding and cash-and-carry arbitrage. The common confusion: in US news, stock futures usually means index futures such as S&P 500 futures, because single stock futures barely trade there.
example: Say ABC Ltd's one-month future trades at ₹1,505 with a lot of 1,000 shares, so one contract is worth ₹15.05 lakh. A trader who sells one contract and buys it back when the future is at ₹1,460 earns (1,505 − 1,460) × 1,000 = ₹45,000 before costs.
formula: Profit on a short contract = (Entry price − Exit price) × Lot size

short: An exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed amount of one currency for another at a set exchange rate on a future date.
kid: You and a friend agree today how many of your shells you will swap for her pebbles next month. Even if pebbles get harder to find, the promise stays the same.
detail: Currency futures are standardised contracts on an exchange rate, such as USD-INR, with fixed contract sizes and expiry dates, cleared through a clearing corporation. Importers, exporters and borrowers use them to lock in a rate, and traders use them to take a view on currency moves. In India, USD-INR futures began trading on NSE in August 2008, with EUR-INR, GBP-INR and JPY-INR contracts added later; they are cash-settled in rupees, and the RBI and SEBI jointly oversee the segment, with RBI rules (as of 2025) requiring users to have a genuine underlying currency exposure. Globally, CME lists the major currency futures, though most corporate hedging still happens through OTC forwards with banks. A common confusion: a currency future is not a forward. Both fix a future rate, but futures are standardised, exchange-traded and marked to market daily, while forwards are private contracts that can match any amount and date.
example: Say ABC Ltd, an importer, must pay $50,000 in three months and buys 50 USD-INR futures of $1,000 each at ₹85.00, locking in ₹42,50,000. If the rupee weakens to ₹86.50 by expiry, buying the dollars costs ₹43,25,000, but the futures gain (86.50 − 85.00) × 50,000 = ₹75,000, bringing the net cost back to ₹42,50,000.
formula: Futures rate ≈ Spot rate × (1 + Domestic interest rate × t) / (1 + Foreign interest rate × t)

short: An exchange-traded contract tied to a government bond or a short-term interest rate, used to hedge against or bet on interest-rate moves.
kid: When you borrow a friend's bike, you give her some sweets as a thank-you. You both agree today how many sweets it will be next month, so nobody gets a surprise.
detail: Interest rate futures (IRFs) let investors lock in a future bond price or interest rate. Bond futures, such as US Treasury futures or Indian futures on 10-year government securities, are priced off a government bond; short-rate futures, such as SOFR or fed funds futures, track an overnight or term rate and are quoted as 100 minus the rate. Because bond prices fall when yields rise, selling bond futures gains when rates go up, so banks, insurers and mutual funds use them to hedge bond portfolios, and their prices reveal what markets expect from central banks. In India, IRFs trade on NSE and BSE but remain small next to the OTC overnight indexed swap market, which most banks prefer for hedging. A common confusion: buying interest rate futures is a bet that rates will fall, not rise, because their prices move opposite to rates.
example: Say a bank holds ₹10 crore of 10-year government bonds and sells interest rate futures covering the same value to hedge. If yields rise and bond prices fall 2%, the bonds lose ₹20 lakh; if the futures price also falls 2%, the short futures gain ₹20 lakh, offsetting the loss.
formula: Short-rate futures price = 100 − Implied interest rate (in %)

short: An agreement on an exchange to buy or sell a set amount of a raw material, like gold or wheat, at a fixed price later.
kid: A farmer and a baker agree in spring on what the baker will pay for wheat after harvest. Then neither of them worries if the price jumps or drops.
detail: Commodity futures are standardised exchange-traded contracts on physical goods: energy such as crude oil and natural gas, metals such as gold, silver and copper, and farm products such as wheat, cotton and soybean. Producers sell futures to lock in prices for their output, users such as refiners, jewellers and food companies buy them to fix input costs, and speculators add liquidity. Many contracts allow delivery to approved warehouses, though most positions are closed before expiry. Prices across expiry months form a curve in contango or backwardation, depending on storage costs and supply tightness. In India, MCX leads in energy and metals and NCDEX in farm goods; SEBI has regulated commodity derivatives since the Forward Markets Commission merged into it in 2015, and has at times suspended sensitive farm contracts. A common confusion: futures prices are not simple forecasts of spot prices, since they also reflect carry costs.
example: Say a farmer expects 10 tonnes (100 quintals) of a crop and sells futures at ₹6,000 per quintal, locking in ₹6,00,000. If the price falls to ₹5,400 at harvest and the futures converge to it, he sells the crop for ₹5,40,000 but gains (6,000 − 5,400) × 100 = ₹60,000 on the futures, so he still receives ₹6,00,000 in total.
formula: Futures price = Spot price × e^((r + u − y) × T), where r = financing rate, u = storage cost rate, y = convenience yield, T = time to expiry in years

short: A contract in which two parties agree to exchange a series of payments over time, such as fixed interest for interest that changes.
kid: You give your friend one sweet every Monday, and she gives you a cookie every Monday. You keep swapping like this for many weeks because you are both happy.
detail: A swap is an over-the-counter derivative in which two parties exchange cash flows, calculated on a notional amount under agreed rules, over a period of time. The main types are interest rate swaps (fixed against floating rates), currency swaps (principal and interest in two currencies), commodity swaps (a fixed price against the market price of, say, fuel), credit default swaps (a premium for default protection) and total return swaps. Companies use swaps to change the nature of their debt or hedge input costs without refinancing, banks use them to manage balance-sheet risk, and investors use them to gain or shed exposure cheaply. Swaps are documented under ISDA master agreements, and since the 2008 crisis many standardised swaps must be centrally cleared. In India, the MIBOR overnight indexed swap dominates. A common confusion: in most swaps the notional amount never changes hands; only the net payments do.
example: Say XYZ Airways, a hypothetical airline, agrees with a bank to pay a fixed $80 a barrel on 100,000 barrels of fuel a month and receive the market price. If the market averages $90 one month, the bank pays the airline (90 − 80) × 100,000 = $1,000,000, offsetting its higher fuel bill; if the market averages $75, the airline pays the bank $500,000.

short: An agreement in which one side pays a fixed interest rate and the other a changing rate on the same agreed sum.
kid: You promise to give your friend three sweets every week. She promises to give you as many sweets as the weather says, some weeks more and some fewer, and you just hand over the difference.
detail: An interest rate swap (IRS) is a contract in which two parties exchange interest payments on a notional principal: one pays a fixed rate and the other a floating rate linked to a benchmark such as SOFR in the US or MIBOR in India. The notional is not exchanged; on each payment date only the net difference is settled. A plain vanilla, fixed-for-floating swap lets a company with floating-rate debt lock in a fixed cost, or one with fixed-rate debt benefit if rates fall, without refinancing. Banks use swaps to manage rate risk, and swap rates form a key yield curve. The fixed rate is set so the swap is worth zero at the start; afterwards its value moves with rates. A common confusion: the party paying fixed gains when rates rise, not when they fall, because the floating rate it receives has gone up.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹100 crore floating-rate loan and enters a swap paying a fixed 7% and receiving the floating rate on ₹100 crore notional, settled yearly. If the floating rate for a year is 6.5%, ABC pays the bank (7% − 6.5%) × ₹100 crore = ₹50 lakh; if it is 7.8%, the bank pays ABC ₹80 lakh. Either way ABC's borrowing cost stays at 7% plus its loan spread.
formula: Net payment to the fixed-rate payer = (Floating rate − Fixed rate) × Notional × Accrual period in years

short: An interest rate swap where one side pays a fixed rate and the other pays the overnight rate, such as MIBOR, compounded over the period.
kid: Every night a sweet jar gives out a different number of sweets. You and a friend agree that one of you gets a steady number and the other gets whatever the jar gives, and you settle up at the end.
detail: An overnight indexed swap (OIS) is an interest rate swap whose floating leg is the daily compounded overnight rate over the swap's life: MIBOR in India, SOFR in the US, €STR in the euro area. At maturity, or periodically for longer swaps, the parties settle the difference between the fixed rate and the compounded overnight rate on the notional. Because overnight rates closely track the central bank's policy rate, OIS rates show what the market expects that rate to average over the coming months or years; analysts read the one-year MIBOR OIS as a gauge of expected RBI moves. In India, MIBOR OIS is the most liquid rupee interest rate derivative, and OIS curves also serve as near risk-free discount curves. A common confusion: the OIS rate is not a rate anyone actually borrows at; it is the fixed rate that makes the swap fair today.
example: Say a bank receives a fixed 6.50% in a one-year OIS on ₹100 crore notional. If overnight MIBOR, compounded over the year, works out to 6.30%, the bank receives (6.50% − 6.30%) × ₹100 crore = ₹20 lakh at maturity.
formula: Net payment to the fixed receiver = (Fixed rate − Compounded overnight rate) × Notional × Days / 365, where Compounded rate = [Product of (1 + r_i × d_i / 365) − 1] × 365 / Days

short: An agreement where two parties exchange a loan amount and its interest in two different currencies, then hand the amounts back at the end.
kid: You lend your friend your toy car and she lends you her doll. Each week you both give a small treat for looking after the other's toy, and at the end you give the toys back.
detail: A currency swap, or cross-currency swap, is an OTC contract in which two parties exchange principal in two currencies at the start, pay each other interest in those currencies over the life of the deal, and re-exchange the same principal amounts at maturity at the original exchange rate. Each interest leg can be fixed or floating. Indian companies that raise dollar loans or bonds abroad often swap them into rupees to remove exchange-rate risk, and foreign borrowers raising rupees do the reverse. Because the final exchange uses the starting rate, the swap locks in the home-currency cost of foreign debt. Pricing includes the cross-currency basis, a spread reflecting demand for dollar funding. A common confusion: a cross-currency swap is not an FX swap, a short spot-plus-forward trade such as the RBI's dollar-rupee buy/sell swaps, nor a central bank swap line, which is an emergency facility between central banks.
example: Say ABC Ltd borrows $10 million abroad and swaps it with a bank at ₹85 per dollar: it hands over $10 million and receives ₹85 crore. Over the swap's life ABC pays rupee interest on ₹85 crore and receives dollar interest on $10 million to service its loan. At maturity the two sides swap back ₹85 crore and $10 million, whatever the market rate is then.

short: A contract where one party gets all the gains and income of an asset without owning it, and pays a financing fee plus any losses.
kid: Your friend keeps a toy in her room but lets you have all the fun and treats that come with it. In return you give her a sweet each week, and if the toy breaks, you pay.
detail: A total return swap (TRS) transfers the full economic performance of a reference asset, such as a share, bond, loan or index, from one party to another. The total return payer, usually a bank that holds the asset as a hedge, passes on all price gains plus dividends or coupons; the receiver pays a floating financing rate plus a spread and covers any fall in value. An equity swap is a TRS on shares or an equity index. The receiver gets leveraged exposure without buying the asset. Because the bank, not the investor, appears as the shareholder, a TRS can hide who economically controls a large stake. The 2021 collapse of Archegos Capital, which built huge concentrated positions through total return swaps with banks, cost those banks more than $10 billion. A common confusion: the TRS receiver bears the risk but usually gets no voting rights.
example: Say a hedge fund enters a one-year total return swap with a bank on $50 million of a stock and pays a 6% financing rate ($3 million). If the stock rises 10% and pays a 2% dividend, the fund receives $6 million and nets $3 million. If the stock falls 20%, the fund pays the bank the $10 million drop plus the $3 million financing.
formula: Receiver's net gain = (Price change + Income on the asset) − (Financing rate + Spread) × Notional × Period

short: An option that gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to enter an interest rate swap on agreed terms at a future date.
kid: You give a friend one sticker so that next month you may swap sweets with her the way you agree today. If you no longer want to by then, you simply don't, and only lose the sticker.
detail: A swaption is an OTC option on an interest rate swap. A payer swaption gives the right to enter a swap paying a fixed rate (the strike) and receiving floating, so it gains value if rates rise; a receiver swaption gives the right to receive fixed and pay floating, so it gains if rates fall. The buyer pays an upfront premium, and the option's expiry and the length of the underlying swap are quoted together, for example a one-year into five-year swaption. Companies use payer swaptions to cap the cost of planned future borrowing, banks and insurers use them to hedge prepayment and call features in mortgages and bonds, and dealers trade them to express views on interest-rate volatility. A common confusion: exercising a swaption usually does not pay a single lump sum; it creates a swap that runs for years, unless the contract specifies cash settlement.
example: Say ABC Ltd pays ₹50 lakh for a one-year payer swaption on ₹100 crore notional with a 7% strike. If a year later the market swap rate is 8%, it exercises and pays 7% fixed instead of 8%, saving 1% × ₹100 crore = ₹1 crore a year over the swap's life. If rates are below 7%, it lets the swaption lapse and loses only the ₹50 lakh premium.
formula: Payer swaption payoff at expiry ≈ max(Market swap rate − Strike rate, 0) × Notional × Annuity factor

short: The reference amount used to calculate a contract's payments, or the full value of what it controls, as opposed to the cash actually paid.
kid: You and a friend count a hundred marbles to work out a game's score, but at the end only two marbles change hands. The hundred is just the counting number.
detail: Notional value is the reference amount underlying a derivative. For futures it is the contract price times the lot size, the total value of the asset controlled; for swaps it is the notional principal on which payments are calculated and which, in most cases, is never exchanged. Notional value shows the scale of exposure and is used for position limits, margin rules, fees and market statistics; BIS surveys put global OTC derivatives at hundreds of trillions of dollars in notional terms. Indian exchange turnover is often quoted in notional terms, which for options can be hundreds of times the premium actually paid. The common confusion is to treat notional as money at risk. A swap on ₹500 crore notional may have a market value of only a few crore, and a futures trader posts just a fraction of notional as margin, though losses can exceed that margin.
example: Say a trader buys one index futures contract at 20,000 with a lot of 50 units: its notional value is 20,000 × 50 = ₹10 lakh, though the margin posted may be about ₹1.2 lakh. Similarly, an interest rate swap on ₹500 crore notional where the two rates differ by 0.25% produces a yearly net payment of just ₹1.25 crore.
formula: Notional value of a futures contract = Futures price × Lot size

short: Contracts whose value depends on another asset, agreed privately between two parties such as a bank and a company, instead of on an exchange.
kid: Instead of swapping toys at the big school fair where everyone watches, two friends make a special promise just between themselves, with their own rules.
detail: Over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives are forwards, swaps, options and other contracts arranged bilaterally, such as between a dealer bank and a client, instead of on an exchange. Their main advantage is flexibility: amount, maturity, underlying and payment terms can be tailored to a company's exact exposure. The costs are less transparency, less liquidity and counterparty risk, because each side depends on the other to pay. After the 2008 crisis, when AIG's huge book of OTC credit default swaps needed a government rescue, G20 reforms required standardised OTC derivatives to be centrally cleared, trades to be reported, and uncleared trades to be margined. In India, the RBI regulates OTC interest rate and currency derivatives, and CCIL clears many rupee swaps and forex forwards. Documentation usually follows the ISDA Master Agreement. A common confusion: OTC does not mean unregulated, and globally OTC markets dwarf exchange markets in notional amount outstanding.
example: Say ABC Ltd must pay exactly $2 million to a supplier in 97 days. Its bank offers an OTC forward for that amount and date at ₹85.40, locking the cost at 2,000,000 × 85.40 = ₹17.08 crore, a match that standard exchange contracts with fixed sizes and expiry dates cannot provide.

short: Standard contracts, such as futures and options, traded on a regulated exchange, where a central clearing body guarantees that every trade is honoured.
kid: At the school fair, everyone swaps the same-sized bags of marbles at one big table, and a teacher makes sure every promise is kept.
detail: Exchange-traded derivatives (ETDs) are futures and options listed on an exchange with standardised terms: underlying, lot size, expiry dates, strike prices and settlement method are all set by the exchange. Orders are matched electronically with transparent prices, and a clearing corporation becomes the counterparty to both sides, collecting initial and mark-to-market margin daily so that one trader's default does not hit others. This makes ETDs liquid and accessible to retail investors, but less tailored than OTC contracts. In India, most ETD volume by number of contracts is in equity index options on NSE and BSE, with smaller activity in stock futures, currency and interest rate contracts, and commodities on MCX and NCDEX; NSE has topped global rankings of derivatives exchanges by contracts traded in recent years. A common confusion: headline turnover figures are notional, while the money actually exchanged in options is the far smaller premium.
example: Say a firm wants to hedge $245,500 with exchange-traded USD-INR futures, each for exactly $1,000. It can buy 245 contracts ($245,000) or 246 ($246,000), leaving a $500 mismatch either way, but in return it gets transparent prices and the clearing corporation's guarantee.

short: An institution that steps between the buyer and seller of every trade, becoming buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, to guarantee settlement.
kid: When two children swap toys, a teacher stands in the middle and takes each toy first. If one child runs off, the teacher still makes sure the other gets a toy.
detail: A central counterparty (CCP) is a clearing house that places itself between the two sides of a trade through novation, so each trader's contract is with the CCP rather than with each other. It protects itself with margins and a default waterfall: the defaulter's initial margin and default-fund contribution are used first, then a slice of the CCP's own capital, then contributions from surviving members. By netting positions and managing defaults centrally, CCPs cut counterparty risk across the market, and after the 2008 crisis G20 reforms required standardised OTC swaps to be cleared through them. In India, NSE Clearing and Indian Clearing Corporation clear exchange trades, and CCIL clears government securities, forex and rupee swap trades. A common confusion: a CCP concentrates risk rather than eliminating it, so its own safety is crucial and regulators treat CCPs as systemically important institutions.
example: Say trader A buys a futures contract on 500 units at ₹1,000 from trader B. After novation the CCP is the seller to A and the buyer to B. If the price rises to ₹1,040 and B defaults, the CCP still pays A the ₹20,000 gain, first using B's margin and then, if needed, its default fund.

short: The risk that the other party to a contract fails to pay or deliver what it owes before the deal is fully settled.
kid: You lend your friend a toy and she promises to give you a sticker next week. If she moves away before then, you never get the sticker.
detail: Counterparty risk, or counterparty credit risk (CCR), is the possibility that the party on the other side of a financial contract defaults before meeting its obligations. It matters most in OTC derivatives and repos, where exposure changes with market prices: a swap that is worth money to you today is only valuable if your counterparty survives to pay. Firms manage it with credit limits, collateral and margin agreements, netting and central clearing, and banks also hold capital and book a credit valuation adjustment against it. The failure of Lehman Brothers in 2008 showed how unpaid derivative contracts can spread losses across the system. A common confusion: counterparty risk is two-way and changes daily. Unlike a loan, where only the lender is exposed, in a derivative either side may end up being owed money, so exposure must be measured as a potential future amount, not only today's value.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a forward contract under which, at today's prices, Bank X owes it ₹3 crore. If Bank X collapses before settlement and creditors recover 40%, ABC gets ₹1.2 crore and loses ₹3 crore × (1 − 0.40) = ₹1.8 crore.
formula: Expected loss = Exposure at default × Probability of default × (1 − Recovery rate)

short: Combining all the amounts two parties owe each other into one payment, so only the difference between them changes hands.
kid: You owe your friend five sweets and she owes you three. Instead of passing eight sweets back and forth, you just give her two.
detail: Netting offsets obligations between parties so that only a net amount is paid or claimed. Payment netting combines payments due on the same day in the same currency into one transfer, cutting settlement risk and the cash needed. Close-out netting, the more important form, applies when a party defaults: all outstanding contracts under a master agreement are terminated, valued and combined into a single net amount, which stops a bankrupt party's administrator from collecting what it is owed while delaying what it owes. Netting can shrink gross exposure dramatically, which is why it is central to ISDA documentation, clearing houses and bank capital rules. India gave close-out netting legal backing through the Bilateral Netting of Qualified Financial Contracts Act, 2020, letting banks measure exposures on a net rather than gross basis. A common confusion: netting only protects you if it is legally enforceable in the defaulting party's insolvency.
example: Say Bank A owes Bank B ₹50 crore on one contract, while B owes A ₹30 crore and ₹15 crore on two others. If B defaults, close-out netting turns these into one amount: A owes B ₹50 crore − ₹30 crore − ₹15 crore = ₹5 crore. Without netting, A might have to pay B's administrator ₹50 crore while waiting in line as a creditor for the ₹45 crore it is owed.
formula: Net amount = Total owed to you − Total you owe

short: A standard contract, published by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, that sets the legal terms for all private derivative trades between two parties.
kid: Two friends write one big rule sheet before they ever swap toys. After that, each new swap just needs a small note, because the big rules already cover everything.
detail: The ISDA Master Agreement is the standard legal framework for OTC derivatives, published by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, an industry body founded in 1985. Two parties sign it once, with a Schedule that customises its choices, and each later trade is recorded in a short confirmation that becomes part of the same single agreement. It sets out payment mechanics, events of default and termination events, and how all trades are closed out and netted if one party fails; a Credit Support Annex usually governs collateral. The 1992 and 2002 versions are both widely used. Its single-agreement structure is what makes close-out netting enforceable, which is why banks worldwide, including Indian banks dealing with foreign counterparties, rely on it. ISDA also publishes standard product definitions. A common confusion: ISDA is a trade association, not a regulator, and signing the master agreement does not by itself create any trade.
example: Say a bank and ABC Ltd sign one ISDA Master Agreement and then do 40 trades over five years, each recorded in a short confirmation. If ABC defaults while trades worth ₹12 crore to the bank and ₹4 crore to ABC are outstanding, all are closed out into one net claim: ABC owes the bank ₹12 crore − ₹4 crore = ₹8 crore.

short: The amount knocked off a contract's value to allow for the chance that the other side fails to pay what it owes.
kid: If a friend who sometimes forgets promises you a sticker, that promise is worth a bit less than the same promise from a friend who always remembers.
detail: Credit valuation adjustment (CVA) is the market value of counterparty credit risk on a derivatives portfolio: the difference between its risk-free value and its value allowing for the counterparty's possible default. It is estimated from expected future exposure, the counterparty's default probability (often implied from CDS spreads) and the loss given default, summed over the life of the trades and discounted. Banks report CVA in their accounts and, under Basel III, hold capital against swings in it, because roughly two-thirds of counterparty-related losses in the 2008 crisis came from falling CVA rather than actual defaults. CVA is the best known of the XVAs, alongside DVA (own default risk), FVA (funding) and KVA (capital). Collateral and netting reduce it. A common confusion: CVA is not a provision for a loss that has already happened; it is a fair-value charge that moves daily with credit spreads even when nobody defaults.
example: Say a bank expects a counterparty to owe it ₹10 crore on a swap if a default occurs, puts the chance of default over the swap's life at 5%, and expects to recover 40%. CVA ≈ ₹10 crore × 5% × (1 − 0.40) = ₹30 lakh, so the bank values the swap ₹30 lakh below its risk-free value.
formula: CVA ≈ (1 − Recovery rate) × Sum over future periods of [Discounted expected exposure × Probability of default in that period]

short: Ready-made investments that combine a bond with a contract linked to an index or asset, so the payout follows preset rules.
kid: Imagine a gift box that holds your coin plus a little game. If the game goes your way you get a treat as well, and the rules are written on the lid.
detail: Structured products are packaged investments, usually notes or debentures issued by a bank or NBFC, whose payoff is linked to an underlying such as an equity index, a share basket, an interest rate or a commodity. Typically they combine a zero-coupon bond, which provides some capital protection, with options that generate the market-linked return, producing features such as partial participation in gains, caps or barriers. In India, the main form is market-linked debentures (MLDs), listed debentures regulated by SEBI and sold mostly to wealthy investors; under the rules as of 2025, the Finance Act 2023 taxes their gains as short-term capital gains at slab rates, and issuance fell sharply after that change. Investors face issuer credit risk, opaque pricing and poor liquidity before maturity. A common confusion: capital protection holds only at maturity and only if the issuer stays solvent; selling early or an issuer default can mean losses.
example: Say a three-year note of ₹10 lakh from XYZ Finance Ltd returns the principal plus 60% of any rise in the Nifty 50. If the index rises 25%, the investor receives ₹10 lakh + 60% × 25% × ₹10 lakh = ₹11.5 lakh. If the index falls, the investor gets back ₹10 lakh, provided the issuer does not default.

short: A market where assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery and payment at today's price, rather than on a future date.
kid: At the corner shop you hand over a coin and get your sweet right away. Nobody promises anything for later.
detail: The spot market, also called the cash market, is where financial instruments and commodities are traded for immediate settlement at the current spot price. Immediate follows market convention: Indian shares settle on T+1 (as of 2025), spot foreign exchange usually settles in two business days, and physical commodities are delivered promptly. Derivatives are priced off the spot market: a futures price equals the spot price adjusted for the cost of carry, and the two converge at expiry. In India, the equity cash segment of NSE and BSE is the spot market for shares, and news often contrasts cash market turnover with F&O turnover. A common confusion: the spot price is not the same as the price of the nearest futures contract, and a spot rate in bond markets means a zero-coupon yield, which is a different idea from the spot market.
example: Say you buy 100 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹250 in the NSE cash market: you pay ₹25,000 and receive the shares in your demat account the next trading day under the T+1 cycle in force as of 2025. A one-month futures contract on the same stock might trade at ₹252, a little above the spot price.

short: A trade, usually run with borrowed money, that buys a bond and sells the matching futures to earn the small price gap between them.
kid: You buy a toy for five coins today and promise to sell it next week for a tiny bit more. You borrowed the coins, so even a little wobble can hurt.
detail: A basis trade exploits the difference, or basis, between the price of a cash asset and its futures contract. In the Treasury basis trade, hedge funds buy US Treasury bonds and sell Treasury futures, which often trade slightly rich because asset managers prefer futures for interest-rate exposure; the fund finances the bonds in the repo market and holds them until futures delivery, when prices converge. Profits per trade are tiny, so funds use very high leverage, often borrowing almost the whole bond value. The trade supplies liquidity and keeps futures and cash prices aligned, but regulators worry about it: they have linked forced unwinds, when repo funding or margins tightened, to the Treasury market turmoil of March 2020. Crypto markets run a similar trade with bitcoin. A common confusion: it is often called arbitrage, but leverage, margin calls and repo funding risk make it far from risk-free.
example: Say a hedge fund buys Treasury bonds for $98 million and sells futures that lock in a delivery value of $98.5 million, a gap of $500,000. If repo financing until delivery, net of the bonds' coupon income, costs $300,000, the fund keeps about $200,000. But it has borrowed nearly all of the $98 million, so a margin call or repo squeeze can force it to sell at a loss.
formula: Gross basis = Cash bond price − (Futures price × Conversion factor)

short: Caps set by regulators or exchanges on how many derivative contracts one trader, or the whole market, can hold on a single share or commodity.
kid: The teacher says each child may hold only five marbles from the jar and the whole class only fifty, so nobody can grab them all and boss the game.
detail: Position limits cap the open positions that can be held in derivatives on a given underlying, to prevent manipulation, squeezes and dangerous concentration. Limits can apply per client, per trading member and across the whole market. In India, each stock in the F&O segment has a market-wide position limit (MWPL) set by a SEBI formula linked to its free float and cash-market activity; when total open interest crosses 95% of MWPL, the stock enters an F&O ban in which positions may only be reduced, and the ban lifts once open interest falls below 80% (rules as of 2025). Index derivatives and commodities carry their own client and member limits, and in the US the CFTC sets federal limits on major commodity futures. A common confusion: a position limit is not about margin or available money. Even a trader with ample funds cannot go beyond it, and breaches attract penalties.
example: Say a stock's market-wide position limit is 10 crore shares. Under the rules as of 2025, once open interest crosses 95% of that, or 9.5 crore shares, the stock enters the F&O ban, and new positions are barred until open interest drops below 80%, or 8 crore shares.
